Successfully implementing innovations requires mastery of many traits including technological excellence, organizational capabilities and good customer relations. Firms however do not perform these tasks in isolation, they depend on innovation policy activities at the EU-, country and regional level as well as on other firms in ecosystems and value chains. Firms are embedded in an institutionalized framework of rules, policies and regulations, which can both limit and enable the innovation process. Examples are abundant, such as firms active in electric vehicles, batteries, steel making, financial industry, chemical industry, food, nanotech, AI, and so on. Knowing and taking advantage of these policies is therefore vital for any innovation active firm, in their open innovation strategies. This course aims to provide students with a broader perspective on innovation, especially when it comes to innovation policy, supporting structures and innovation strategies which could be important knowledge for them to take forward into their professional lives, such as in technical and management consultancy. It also provides some alternative academic perspectives ranging from innovation management to social sciences and policy studies, which will bring new perspectives to their understanding of innovation and its contemporary societal, economic, and political importance. Specifically, students will have an understanding of what kinds of innovation policies and supports exist at the local, regional, national, and European levels, and how these are accessed. They will also gain an understanding of how other policy areas and regulations, such as IP protection, venture capital, tax systems, and wider economic development policy, influence the innovation system. The course also provides a critical view on innovation, giving students the tools to also question its predominance in policy and wider societal debates.

The course contains 7 weeks of teaching, and one week devoted to the individual written exam
Weekly themes:
Introduction - Innovation in a wider perspective.
Role of state (and different actors) in the innovation system.
Innovation policy- European, national, and regional.
Innovation and Sustainability, regulatory environment.
Intellectual property, tax systems, procurement, government support.
Financing Innovation - Venture Capital (public and private).
Group Project Work & Presentations
Individual reading logs

Grading scale: TH - (U, 3, 4, 5) - (Fail, Three, Four, Five)
Assessment:

For final grades, an approved project report, approved individual written exam and active participation in seminars are required. 1) Project report (Group based)- Taking an innovation from idea to implementation-how to navigate the innovation ecosystem. Groups identify a real-life innovation (firm based) and write a report on how the innovation could be supported or challenged by the policy and regulatory environment, and which systemic perspective needs to be taken into account when taking an innovation from idea to reality. 2) Individual Written Exam- Reading log- throughout the course students make reflections on the course reading, relating what they have read to their previous knowledge and experiences around innovation, and taking a critical perspective to discuss the literature in an evaluative manner. The log should cover all of the course readings provided. 3) Active Participation in Seminars- If seminars are missed written make up tasks must be submitted.

The examiner, in consultation with Disability Support Services, may deviate from the regular form of examination in order to provide a permanently disabled student with a form of examination equivalent to that of a student without a disability.
